sentences.text: Rahonavis was a small predator roughly 70 centimeters long and weighing between 0.45 and 2.27 kilograms.
The animal possessed a long tail, a jaw lined with serrated teeth, and the characteristic retractable claw on the second toe.
Evidence of feathers on the ulna gave the creature an avian appearance.
The name Rahonavis translates to "cloud menace bird," combining Malagasy words for cloud or menace with the Latin word for bird.
A dentary bone has been found associated with the holotype, though it is rarely described in detail.
The only known specimen, a partial skeleton cataloged as UA 8656, was discovered by Catherine Forster and colleagues.
Fossils were first recovered in 1995 by a joint expedition from SUNY and the University of Antananarivo near Berivotra.
The discoverers originally named the genus Rahona but renamed it Rahonavis after finding that Rahona was already used for a genus of moths.
The skeleton consists of articulated hind legs, a torso, parts of the tail, and good remains of the forelimbs and shoulder bones.
It is unclear if Rahonavis could fly, and some doubt exists regarding whether the forearm material with quill knobs belongs to the same skeleton as the rest of the remains.
Luis M. Chiappe argued that Rahonavis could probably fly, citing its large, robust ulna and prominent quill knobs as evidence of larger and more powerful wings than those of Archaeopteryx.
Agnolín and Novas suggested that, similar to Microraptor, Rahonavis likely used a bat-like flight stroke utilizing the deltoideus muscle complexes.
The shoulder bones show evidence of ligament insertions that allow the independent mobility necessary for flapping.
There has been historical uncertainty regarding whether Rahonavis belongs to the bird clade Avialae or is a closely related dromaeosaurid.
Rahonavis belongs to the parent group Unenlagiinae.
The genus is classified within the family Dromaeosauridae.
Rahonavis is classified as a reptile.
Rahonavis lived in northwestern Madagascar during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 70 to 66 million years ago.
It lived during the Maastrichtian stage, between 72.2 and 66 million years ago.
As of 2020, paleontologists remain undecided whether Rahonavis is an unenlagiine, a dromaeosaurid, or an avialan.
There has been historical uncertainty regarding whether Rahonavis is a member of the clade Aves or closely linked to dromaeosaurids.
A 2013 analysis by Agnolin and Novas found Rahonavis closer to Avialae than to Dromaeosauridae.
A 2019 analysis by Hartman et al. strongly rejected the avian position of Rahonavis, supporting its placement in Unenlagiinae as requiring fewer evolutionary steps.
